clue.text: End of short and curlies twisting bladders

indicators.note: twisting tells us the letters of curlies, with one more added, are wound into a new order
End of points to the last letter of the word short

explanation.surface: A coarse remark about pubic hair being twisted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'End of' picks T, the last letter of 'short'; 'twisting' shuffles T with CURLIES to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Utricles are small sacs or bladder-like cavities in plants and animals, so bladders is a fair synonym.

clue.text: Slight bending of rules out East

indicators.note: bending of says the remaining letters of rules are bent out of their order
out tells us a letter is taken out of the word rules

explanation.surface: A minor relaxation of the regulations, except in the East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' removes E (East) from RULES, leaving RULS; 'bending of' rearranges those four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A slur is an insult or slight, a remark that belittles someone; both are nouns here.

clue.text: Rat one slaughtered with some indecision in the forecourt

indicators.note: slaughtered suggests the rat and the one are cut up and reassembled in another order

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
um is the hesitant noise of someone undecided

explanation.surface: A rat is killed in a courtyard while someone dithers over it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slaughtered' rearranges the rat and I (one) to ATRI; the forecourt sense is the open court at the front of a Roman house.
explanation.definitionFit: An atrium is an open central court or entrance hall in front of a building, much like a forecourt.

clue.text: A Kentish rebel, me? Where's your scholarship?

parts.note: Jack Cade led the 1450 rising of Kentish rebels against Henry VI

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether they, a rebel from Kent, could be the seat of learning.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Cade led a popular revolt from Kent (a county in south-east England) in 1450.
explanation.definitionFit: Academe is the world of universities and learned study, the place where scholarship lives.

clue.text: With a heather on board one might get fires

annotationWithheld.why: With a heather on board one might get fires: W + A + LING inside SS, but 'on board' must both give SS and signal the container, one phrase doing two jobs
annotationWithheld.clue: With a heather on board one might get fires

clue.text: Counsellors getting letters from young Santa

indicators.note: letters from suggests the letters of young Santa are taken and rearranged

explanation.surface: Advisers receiving fan mail from a youthful Father Christmas.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'letters' as post, which agony aunts do get; here it means the letters of YOUNG SANTA, rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Agony aunts are newspaper columnists who counsel readers on personal problems sent in by post.

clue.text: Old car's force leaving bundles of nerves

indicators.note: leaving says the force departs from the word for the nerve bundles

parts.note: ganglia are clusters of nerve cells
g is the symbol for gravitational force, as in g-force

explanation.surface: A vintage motor's power has gone, leaving the driver a nervous wreck.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is', linking definition to wordplay. The Ford Anglia was a British family car of the 1940s to 1960s.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ford Anglia is a classic British small car no longer made, so an old car.

clue.text: See 9
Players here waiting the call, almost made it!

indicators.note: made it suggests the letters are fashioned afresh into something new
almost means the word call loses its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone waiting to be summoned nearly managed it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims CALL to CAL; WAITING + THE + CAL is then rearranged ('made it') into the football club's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Wigan Athletic is an English football club, so its home is a place where players are found.

clue.text: Noble utterance where 21's 24 across ends in 9

indicators.note: utterance means the word is spoken, so we want what it sounds like

parts.note: a peer is a noble, a member of the nobility

explanation.surface: A lord speaks about where a famous road finishes.
explanation.walkthrough: 21 is ORWELL and 24 across ROAD: his book The Road to Wigan Pier ends at a pier in Wigan (9).
explanation.definitionFit: Orwell's book title names Wigan's pier, so the structure is where his road ends in Wigan.

clue.text: How to take it easy at home: work fast and play evenly

parts.note: in means at home, as in staying in
do means work, as in doing a job
Lent is the Christian season of fasting

indicators.note: evenly picks the even-numbered letters of play, its second and fourth

explanation.surface: Advice on relaxing at home: fast from work and play at a steady pace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'evenly' takes the 2nd and 4th letters of 'play', L and Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Indolently means lazily, without effort, which describes the manner of someone taking it easy.

clue.text: 8 players here had left beaten, word of contemplation needed outside

indicators.note: needed outside says the word of contemplation wraps around the other letters

parts.note: om is the sacred syllable chanted in meditation

indicators.note: beaten suggests the letters are knocked into a different order

explanation.surface: Athletic players here lost, and a meditative mantra was called for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beaten' gives LDHA; 'needed outside' wraps the mantra round it. 8 is ATHLETIC: Oldham Athletic is a football club.
explanation.definitionFit: Oldham Athletic is an English football club, so Oldham is a home of athletic players.

clue.text: "O, woe indeed, Gloucester!"

definitions.meaning: an exclamation of bad luck, used ironically as 'tough luck'
Double Gloucester is a firm English cheese

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests Shakespeare's Earl of Gloucester lamenting; it is the cheese. Hard cheese is British slang for bad luck.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard cheese means tough luck, a cry of woe; Double Gloucester is literally a hard cheese.

clue.text: Indonesian holding with end of Kipling's 24 across

indicators.note: holding says the Indonesian word contains the other piece

parts.note: Malay is the language and people of Indonesia and Malaysia
and means with, joining things together

explanation.surface: An Indonesian possession tied to where Kipling's journey finishes.
explanation.walkthrough: 24 across is ROAD: Kipling's poem 'Mandalay' speaks of 'the road to Mandalay'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Kipling's poem the road leads to the Burmese city, so the city is that road's end.

clue.text: One dodging the issue with the East German plutocracy

parts.note: Ost is German for East
the plutocracy are the rich, the class ruling by wealth

explanation.surface: Someone avoiding the question in league with East German moneyed elite.
explanation.walkthrough: The bird is popularly said to bury its head in the sand to avoid danger.
explanation.definitionFit: An ostrich, figuratively, is someone who refuses to face unpleasant facts, as the bird supposedly hides its head.

clue.text: 8 players here with sweeper not left standing

parts.note: a char is a cleaning woman, one who sweeps

indicators.note: standing in a down clue means the words not and left are set upright, read from the bottom

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Athletic players here with a defender who has been knocked down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'standing' turns the pair upward in this down clue, giving LTON. Sweeper is also a football position, the misdirection. Charlton Athletic is a London football club.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlton Athletic is an English football club, so Charlton is a home of athletic players.

clue.text: Conversely, what one does at the Portaloo, say, with some accuracy

indicators.note: say means the phrase is heard rather than spelt out

parts.words: Conversely, what one does at the Portaloo
parts.note: at a portable toilet one queues and then pees; conversely puts those two in the other order

explanation.surface: Joke about public toilets and precision.
explanation.walkthrough: A Portaloo is a portable toilet: you queue, then pee. 'Conversely' swaps them to 'pees and queues', which sounds like the letters P and Q.
explanation.definitionFit: Minding your Ps and Qs means taking care over details and manners, a kind of accuracy.

clue.text: "Where to now?", said Spartacus. "Another epic?"

definitions.meaning: Latin for 'whither goest thou?', words of the apostle Peter to Christ
a 1951 Hollywood epic film set in Nero's Rome, as Spartacus is an epic

explanation.walkthrough: Spartacus is itself a Roman epic film, so the other epic is a sister film of ancient Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: Quo Vadis means 'where are you going?' and is also the title of a historical epic film.

clue.text: Old time dancing's beginning inside English halls

parts.note: ex means former, old

indicators.note: inside places the first letter of dancing within the word for time

parts.note: an era is a period of time

indicators.note: beginning picks out the first letter of dancing's

explanation.surface: Old-time dancing starting up in English halls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beginning' gives D, which goes 'inside' the period of time to make EDRA, before the final E.
explanation.definitionFit: Exedrae are classical recesses or halls with seating for conversation, so halls stands for them loosely.

clue.text: Jules et Jim's Jeanne catching canine with some choice scraps

indicators.note: catching means the actress's surname holds the canine letter inside it

parts.note: Jeanne Moreau starred in Truffaut's film Jules et Jim
C stands for canine in dental notation
an X marks a choice on a ballot paper

explanation.surface: A French film star grabs a dog and some tasty leftovers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'catching' puts C inside MOREAU to give MORCEAU; X, the cross marking a choice, completes the plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Morceaux are small pieces or morsels, French for bits, so scraps is a fair synonym.

clue.text: River as alternative water supply

parts.note: or introduces an alternative
a well supplies water

explanation.surface: Using a river as a backup source of water.
explanation.walkthrough: The Orwell is a river in Suffolk, England.
explanation.definitionFit: The Orwell is an English river flowing through Ipswich to the North Sea.

clue.text: Guardian of the Guardian crossword was he?

definitions.meaning: Latin ... means a keeper or warden

definitions.text: of the Guardian crossword was he?
definitions.meaning: a setter's pseudonym used in the Guardian newspaper's crossword

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading asks which compiler kept watch over the Guardian puzzle; one setter there used this Latin name.
explanation.definitionFit: Custos is Latin for keeper or warden, and was also the pen name of a Guardian compiler.

clue.text: Welsh fancy man, I see, losing cool

indicators.note: losing tells us the word fancy sheds part of itself

parts.note: a fan cools you
Mr is the title of a man
C sounds like see

explanation.surface: A Welsh lover catches sight of something and loses his composure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing' takes the cooling device out of the first word, leaving CY. 'Fancy man' looks like one phrase meaning lover, but splits.
explanation.definitionFit: Cymric means Welsh, from Cymru, the Welsh name for Wales.

clue.text: Precious muddle to sort out which twin?

parts.note: twee means affectedly precious

indicators.note: to sort out means the letters of muddle are rearranged

explanation.surface: A dainty confusion over which twin is which.
explanation.walkthrough: TWEE is followed by DLEDUM, the letters of MUDDLE sorted out. Tweedledum and Tweedledee are the near-identical twins of Through the Looking-Glass.
explanation.definitionFit: Tweedledum is one of Lewis Carroll's identical twins, the other being Tweedledee.

parts.note: fill the gap in the title of the book by 21 down about the town at 9 and its pier at 10

explanation.walkthrough: 21 is ORWELL, 9 WIGAN and 10 PIER: the missing word completes Orwell's 1937 book title.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word in Orwell's book title about poverty in northern England is this route word.

clue.text: Galley master's verbal instruction repeated on ferry

indicators.note: repeated means the sound is given twice
verbal means spoken, so we want what is heard

parts.note: the galley master's order to the oarsmen is row

explanation.surface: A slave-ship boss shouts the same order again aboard a ferry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'verbal' gives RO, said like 'row'; 'repeated' doubles it. Ro-ro means roll-on roll-off.
explanation.definitionFit: A ro-ro is a roll-on roll-off ferry, which vehicles drive on and off.

clue.text: Pass out from colossal return of catch

indicators.note: return of says the remaining letters are read backwards
out from tells us the pass is removed from colossal

parts.note: a col is a mountain pass

explanation.surface: Someone faints after an enormous boomerang catch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out from' removes COL (pass) from COLOSSAL to leave OSSAL; 'return of' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: A lasso is a rope with a noose used to catch cattle, so catch fits as a verb.

clue.text: Bill one to syphon off some pollutant

parts.note: AC is short for account, a bill
one is the Roman numeral I
to drain is to draw liquid off

explanation.surface: An invoice for siphoning away some contaminant.
explanation.walkthrough: AC (account, i.e. bill) + I + DRAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Acid rain is precipitation polluted by sulphur and nitrogen oxides, an instance of pollution.
